newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish police brace for Nazi-leftist battle.
newsitem.headline: Danish police brace for Nazi-leftist battle.

text.p: Danish and foreign neo-Nazi groups are to march in a Danish town on Saturday to mark 10 years since the death of Hitler's deputy Rudolf Hess, and police fear a bloody clash with leftist counter-demonstrators.
A force of 800 officers will stream into the usually quiet cathedral town of Roskilde, west of Copenhagen, to keep up to 400 neo-Nazis and 1,000 of their sworn opponents apart.
"We must hope that both sides behave better than last time but we shall plan for the worst eventually, that's why we are deploying so many," Roskilde police chief Uffe Kornerup said.

A 1995 march in the town against the arrest locally of German-American neo-Nazi leader Gary Lauck turned into a rout when neo-Nazis were scattered by a far larger group of leftists who later stoned the buses taking the right-wingers home.
Jonni Hansen, chairman of the Danish National Socialist Movement (DNSB) says he has no confidence in the police to safeguard his marchers this time.
"We don't trust the police, but we are well prepared," he told Reuters. He did not give details.
He said that he expected 200-400 participants on the memorial march. The DNSB is secretive about its strength but is believed to number about 200.

Anti-Nazi groups say that local Hess marchers' numbers will be swollen by allied groups from Norway, Sweden and Germany and from Britain's Combat 18, so called because of the first and eighth letters of the alphabet -- A and H -- the initials of Adolf Hitler.

British media reports last January linked Combat 18 to Danish neo-Nazi Thomas Nakaba, arrested in Denmark on suspicion of planning to send letter bombs to British sports personalities in mixed-race marriages.
Nakaba goes on trial on August 25.

Denmark's liberal freedom of speech laws have made it something of neo-Nazi haven, to the irritation of neighbouring Germany where Nazi tracts and emblems are banned, and to the discomfort of Danes who remember wartime Nazi occupation.
German groups have been able to post banned literature to German addresses from Danish post boxes, including a list of 280 German leftists and liberals to be "punished".

German Nazi apologist Thies Christophersen published books and pamphlets denying the Holocaust from his Danish home close to the German border until forced to move in 1994, at the age of 78, by protest demonstrations.
German police are also bracing for clashes with neo-Nazi groups throughout the weekend of the Hess anniversary.

Hess hanged himself with an electric cord in Berlin's Spandau prison on August 17, 1987, and the date has become a rallying point for the radical right in Germany and other European countries in recent years.

Hess, the private secretary to whom Hitler dictated his political testament Mein Kampf, became deputy Fuehrer in 1932. He was effectively in charge of the Nazi party until 1941, when he parachuted into Scotland on a mysterious mission to press for an Anglo-German alliance against the Soviet Union.
He spent the rest of his life in custody, the last two decades as the sole inmate of Spandau, where many of his admirers say he was murdered by the Allies.
